blindSummary:
This country presents heightened risk for trans visitors: a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence against trans people, but no criminalisation of trans identity and a landmark 17-year conviction for police torture of a trans woman. Congress approved (February-April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated facilities restriction comparable to the toughest measures now in force in some other large destinations. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and intersex people were assassinated (trans women most affected). In a landmark case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025) — the first such conviction in the country's history, in a case that also reached a regional human-rights court. A presidential decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024), but was walked back after massive protests.

For a visitor: no border friction, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure when using public facilities.
blindOutOfScope: General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: News outlet (Feb 2025): a congressional women's-and-family commission in this country unanimously approved a bill barring people from using public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex (two bills sponsored by individual lawmakers); an activist called it discriminatory; it also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage.
University human-rights institute analysis: commentary treating the country's congressional prohibition of trans people accessing public bathrooms as legalised discrimination.

Regional LGBTQ+ news platform (July 2024): hate crimes have increased in this country and trans women are the most affected - 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 rights violations 2020-2023 according to a university human-rights observatory; documents the extortion-killing of a trans sex worker by a criminal gang, with victims' bodies filmed as extortion threats.

A foreign broadcaster's world service (Dec 2025): 17 years' prison for three police officers in this country for raping and torturing a trans woman - the first conviction in the country for discrimination-based sexual torture, and the first case in which a regional human-rights court recognised discrimination-motivated torture anywhere in the region (a 2008 case from a provincial town).

News outlet (Dec 2025): the aggressors receive their sentence almost 20 years later - 17 years' effective imprisonment; the first time the country's justice system convicted state agents for prejudice-motivated sexual torture of an LGBTI person, fulfilling the regional court's reparations measures (the state publicly acknowledged responsibility and apologised in 2022).
An international human-rights organisation (May 2025): a new law in this country uses vague provisions that threaten free speech and trans people's rights.
An international human-rights organisation (Jun 2024): this country's health ministry walks back guidance classifying trans identities as mental-health problems requiring assessment.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): one of the few countries in the region not recognising same-sex couples; trans people can rectify name/gender markers only via an expensive, complicated court process taking years; a 2017 law bans SOGI discrimination but violence persists and hate crimes go unpunished; in 2024 the Health Ministry unexpectedly issued a decree classifying trans identity as a mental-health condition.

Overseas solidarity-group briefing (April 2025): a week of setbacks - congress approved two 2023-session bills banning people from using public bathrooms counter to their birth sex and banning inclusive signage; criticised by the ombudsman's office; part of a broader rollback of gender, LGBTQ+ and reproductive rights.

Activist news digest (May 2017): this country's congress voted 66-29 to remove LGBT terms from hate-crime legislation, repealing the section of a January 2017 presidential decree that had extended hate-crime protections to sexual orientation and gender identity after a million-signature petition; the country returned to being one of three countries in the region with no LGBT anti-discrimination laws.
blindLocalsOnly: The court-based legal-gender-recognition process (expensive, years-long, no self-ID law) is resident-facing; the 54 assassinations and the police-torture conviction concern residents.
